title: History of Economic Thought
description: Original exercises about economic arguments and the assumptions that distinguish them, rather than name-and-date trivia or a chronology of economic events. Prerequisites: introductory microeconomics and macroeconomics, algebra and ratios; basic differentiation supports marginal-utility examples. Conditional expectations and regression concepts help with modern-methodology extensions. Named attributions are tied to primary texts; constructed numerical applications and modern formal reconstructions are labeled as such. The selection covers parts of the classical, marginalist, Marxian, institutional, Keynesian and modern methodological traditions without claiming exhaustive global coverage or a single uncontested account of disciplinary progress.
